title: Can a supplied Karp–Rabin fingerprint be verified in near-linear time?
formal: Given a string $S\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^{n}$ and a prime $q$, with $\sigma,q\le n^{O(1)}$, define $h_q(x_1\cdots x_\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}x_t\sigma^{\ell-t}\bmod q$. Can one decide in $O(n\log n)$ time whether there exist equal-length substrings $A,B$ of $S$ such that $A\ne B$ but $h_q(A)=h_q(B)$? The modulus is part of the input and cannot be replaced. The deterministic decision problem is the precise target here; the source also permits randomized certification that never accepts a colliding modulus and rejects a collision-free one only with small probability.
context:
Rolling fingerprints turn a long substring into one machine-sized value. Prefix hashes let an algorithm obtain that value without reading the substring again. Unequal fingerprints certify unequal strings, but equal fingerprints only suggest equality. A verifier would determine whether that suggestion is reliable simultaneously for every substring length in the particular input.

For example, in the binary string 001110, the length-three substrings 001 and 110 represent the integers 1 and 6. Modulo 5 their fingerprints coincide, although the strings differ. Two occurrences of 001 would not be a collision: positions are allowed to differ, and it is the substring contents that matter.

For a fixed length there are only linearly many substrings, but repeating the check independently over all lengths creates quadratic work. The hoped-for improvement must share information between lengths. Checking only a predetermined pattern or only the substring comparisons actually made by one application supplies a weaker guarantee.

There is an important existing workaround: verify power-of-two lengths, then represent a general substring by a pair of overlapping power-of-two fingerprints. This changes the fingerprint being certified. It does not certify the single supplied polynomial residue at every length, so it does not settle this question.
why: I include this because it separates fast probabilistic equality tests from fast certification of the hash itself. Near-linear verification of a supplied modulus would make a common assumption in string data structures checkable at nearly the cost of reading the input, while clarifying which composite-fingerprint workarounds are actually necessary.
definitions: Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log n)$, enlarged by a fixed constant to hold the polynomially bounded alphabet symbols and modulus. Arithmetic on a constant number of words costs $O(1)$. Substrings may overlap. The quantified lengths range from $1$ through $n$. This is certification for a fixed string and fixed modulus, not a universal collision-free hash for all strings.

progress.text: Karp and Rabin introduce randomized fingerprinting for pattern matching; a short residue supports efficient comparisons but can identify unequal strings.

Navarro surveys an $O(n\log n)$ expected-time construction of a composite collision-free substring fingerprint, formed from two verified power-of-two pieces. Its guarantee concerns the composite representation.
Farach-Colton explicitly asks for linear or $O(n\log n)$ verification of the given prime against all equal-length substring pairs, and records a straightforward quadratic-time solution.

title: Can exact fully dynamic APSP have edge-linear amortized updates and polylogarithmic queries?
formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
context:
Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.
why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

title: An FPRAS for counting undirected Euler tours

Do not confuse Euler tours with Eulerian orientations: approximate counting of the latter has an FPRAS. Fix a tour-counting convention; standard rotation/reversal factors do not affect FPRAS existence.

title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
formal: Given adjacency-list oracle access to two bounded-degree n-vertex graphs, can one distinguish isomorphism from requiring at least εdn edge changes to become isomorphic using o(n) queries, for every fixed degree bound d and fixed ε>0? context:
The source asks for the full query complexity and gives an n^(2/3) lower bound up to logarithmic factors for two unknown graphs. The first decisive target here is any truly sublinear tester.

title: Is private PAC sample complexity polynomial in VC dimension and log-star Littlestone dimension?
formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every finite Boolean concept class C admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most 1/10 and confidence at least 9/10, while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
context:
VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.
why: The problem seeks a privacy analogue of a foundational characterization theorem in learning theory.

progress.text: The survey gives lower bound $\Omega(\mathrm{VC}+\log^*\mathrm{LD})$ and upper bound $\min\{O(\log|C|),\widetilde O(\mathrm{LD}^5)\}$. The $\mathrm{VC}=1$ case is nearly understood; the general gap remains.

context_blocks.text: VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to {0,1}. VC(C) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. LD(C) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record.
answer_criterion: Prove one polynomial upper bound that works for all finite concept classes under the fixed privacy and learning parameters, or prove that no universal polynomial of these two dimensions suffices. An unspecified new characterization or a smaller bound for one class alone is not a resolution.

importance.reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.

title: Optimal private selection using only Gaussian queries
formal: For a finite set $Y$, public losses $\ell_y$ have sensitivity 1 under a one-record change in the database $X$. The only access to $X$ is through adaptive queries $q_i(X)+N(0,1/(2\rho_i))$, with sensitivity at most 1 and $\sum_i\rho_i\le\rho$. Can the algorithm output $\hat y$ satisfying $\mathbb E[\ell_{\hat y}(X)]-\min_y\ell_y(X)=O(\log|Y|/\sqrt\rho)$?
context:
The exponential mechanism achieves this error with direct data access. The question is whether noise addition alone can exactly match its guarantee.

The goal is to select a nearly best candidate from a finite menu. A candidate might be a hypothesis or a model configuration, and its loss is evaluated on a private database. The algorithm needs one good choice; accurately estimating every candidate’s loss can be much more information than the task requires.

The interface restriction is the substance of the question. The algorithm sees only noisy answers and must split a fixed budget among its queries. Spending less budget on a query increases its Gaussian noise. Adaptively narrowing the candidate set might save information, but later decisions are based on earlier noisy comparisons. The target asks whether that process can lose no asymptotic factor relative to optimal direct selection.
why: It tests equivalence between two basic privacy primitives. The remaining polyloglogarithmic gap is a concrete obstacle to an optimal reduction.

progress.text: The baseline binary-tree method has error $O(\log^{3/2}|Y|/\sqrt\rho)$.
The new algorithm achieves $O(\log|Y|(\log\log|Y|)^{11}/\sqrt\rho)$. Section 1.2 explicitly leaves removal of the $\log\log|Y|$ factor open.

title: Optimal private selection using only Laplace queries
formal: Let $Y$ be a finite set of candidates, each with a public loss function $\ell_y$ of sensitivity one under a one-record database change. To access the database, an algorithm makes $k$ adaptive sensitivity-1 queries. Its answers are $q_i(X)+\mathrm{Lap}(k)$, where $k$ is the scale. Can it guarantee expected excess loss $O(\log|Y|)$ for arbitrary losses? The algorithm may choose the number of queries.
context:
This model corresponds to basic composition for pure privacy. The stronger concentration of Gaussian noise cannot simply be transferred.

Here the menu of candidates is finite and each loss changes by at most one when one database record changes. The algorithm tries to choose a candidate whose expected loss is close to the best available loss. Its only observations are sensitivity-bounded statistical queries with Laplace noise.

Taking more queries is not free in this interface: the noise scale of each answer grows with the total query count k. A method that estimates all losses can spend too much accuracy on candidates that will never be selected. A method that repeatedly eliminates candidates risks making irreversible choices from noisy comparisons. The problem asks whether a carefully organized query process can still reach logarithmic excess loss.
why: The cost of pure privacy is a structural model distinction, rather than an arbitrary change of constants. It determines the reach of noise addition as a universal primitive.

progress.text: The binary-tree algorithm has error $O(\log^2|Y|)$.
The authors explain why their nearly optimal Gaussian method does not yield a tight Laplace bound and leave this model open.

title: Is containment of conjunctive queries under bag semantics decidable?
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries q_1 and q_2 with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and D(A_j[h]) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function U^r to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
context:
Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let q(x) have body R(x), and let r(x) have body R(x),R(x). If R(a) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns m^2. Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as m=2. This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.
why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.

progress.text: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper.

Marcinkowski and Orda prove undecidability for nearby generalizations, including comparison after a supplied linear transformation of a Boolean query’s count. This is not the unmodified containment predicate.
Konstantinidis and Mogavero prove decidability when the left query is join-on-free and the right query is a general CQ. This extends the earlier projection-free decidable case.
The revised Marcinkowski–Ostropolski-Nalewaja paper develops techniques connecting CQ and UCQ containment, while explicitly leaving ordinary CQ-versus-CQ bag-containment decidability open.
Amarilli’s maintained question list continues to list bag-containment decidability. Current searches did not locate a resolution of the plain two-CQ formulation.

title: Does naive evaluation over p-stable semirings converge in O((p+1)n) rounds?
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer p>=0, every n>=1, every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map F:S^n -> S^n with coefficients in S? Starting with x^(0)=(0,...,0), perform synchronous iteration x^(t+1)=F(x^(t)). There must exist an integer t<=C(p+1)n with x^(t+1)=x^(t). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.
definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times a=0. No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and a^0=1. Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by (p+1)n is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
context:
In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only O(n), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma p n^2 (n^2 log(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for O((p+1)n), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. The inspected listings supply no theorem or accessible manuscript for that entry. This card therefore preserves the precise historical question with an uncertain current status; the title alone does not identify which convergence bound, iteration scheme, or semiring hypotheses it settles.
why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.

importance.reason: A foundational convergence question for semiring-valued recursion, with implications beyond one query language. Its historical significance is high, but a newly announced directly relevant paper makes current open status uncertain.

progress.text: Work on convergence of Datalog over pre-semirings establishes stable-semiring convergence and an exponential upper bound in the number of grounded coordinates; the later polynomial paper reviews this starting point.
Im, Moseley, Ngo, and Pruhs establish polynomial convergence for nonlinear programs. The inspected arXiv v2 states the additional sigma and lambda dependencies explicitly.
Ngo records the gap between the polynomial upper bound and Omega((p+1)n), and proposes a matching linear upper bound.

Author publication pages list Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo, with a forthcoming PODS 2027 label on Ngo’s page. No theorem text was obtained for that entry. Its relationship to this exact target requires verification.

title: A problem on unambiguous DNFs
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal: This source pointer refers to the weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs. The full statement, binary-weight convention, decision target, progress, and importance assessment are on TCS-0310. This retained record is not counted as a second mathematical problem.
context:
The catalogue originally acquired this topic by two routes. TCS-0310 came from Antoine Amarilli’s maintained list, under weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs. TCS-0485 came from the 2024 Dagstuhl report on database representation, provenance, and explanations. Inspecting the latter’s Section 6.1 shows that its entire problem contribution is a pointer to Monet’s question numbered 53733 on Theoretical Computer Science Stack Exchange.

That original question supplies an explicitly listed unambiguous DNF, binary-encoded nonnegative integer weights, and an objective maximizing the weight of an assignment that falsifies the formula. It also gives the equivalent threshold decision formulation. Amarilli’s entry links to the same question and describes the same computational task. Using an at-least threshold instead of a strict integer threshold only shifts the threshold by one; it does not create a separate complexity question.

The overlap was checked through the primary link rather than inferred from similar titles. The seminar record does not introduce a special graph representation, a different source of weights, or a restriction that would merit its own card. Its provenance remains useful as evidence that the problem was discussed at the seminar. The original ID is therefore retained, along with its bibliography and any personal browser notes, and its related-card link leads to the completed canonical formulation. Any future refinement with a substantively different mathematical target should be stated explicitly before being counted separately.
why: The question’s significance is explained on TCS-0310. Keeping this bibliographic pointer preserves provenance, while marking the duplicate prevents repeated appearances from inflating the collection’s number of distinct problems.
status_note: Duplicate of TCS-0310. The seminar entry links directly to Monet’s original weighted-falsifiability question, also used by the earlier catalogue record. It introduces no different formula class, weight encoding, or complexity target.

progress.text: Section 6.1 identifies the problem solely by a link to Monet’s question 53733.
The primary links and formulations were compared individually; the complete card is TCS-0310.

title: Determining the sixth Busy Beaver value BB(6)
formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$, the maximum number of steps taken before halting by a deterministic Turing machine with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols, and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape. The transition into a separate halting state counts as one step. Thus $BB(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal{M}_6\text{ halts on the blank tape}\}$, where $T(M)$ counts executed transitions and the machine class is fixed below.
definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in T(M). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$.
answer_criterion: Give an explicit positive integer N and prove BB(6)=N: exhibit a machine in the stated class that halts after exactly N transitions, and prove that every halting machine in this class takes at most N transitions. A finite, unambiguous expression using explicitly defined total operations is sufficient to specify N; its decimal expansion is not required. A larger lower bound or the analysis of only some remaining machines does not settle the question.
context:
Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved S(5)=47,176,870 with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.
why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

importance.reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.

title: Universality of Turing equivalence

Distinguish Turing equivalence from arithmetic equivalence, whose universality is known, and from uniform universality, which is a different restriction.

why: Asks whether equality of computational power can represent every countable Borel classification problem, a classical bridge between computability and descriptive set theory.

title: Erdős girth conjecture: is the classical spanner size bound tight?
formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
context:
High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.
why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.

progress.text: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size.

Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.

title: Does P≠NP imply a samplable NP problem outside AvgP?
formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
answer_criterion: Prove or disprove the displayed implication for ordinary Turing computation. A positive answer must derive existence of a pair (L,D) outside the precisely defined AvgP from P≠NP alone. Hardness under an arbitrary uncomputable distribution, a conjecture about one particular random-instance model, or a reduction requiring additional hardness assumptions does not establish this implication. A relativized separation only limits relativizing proof methods.
context:
Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.
why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.

title: Does average-case NP hardness imply infinitely-often one-way functions?
formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant c>0, infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
context:
Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption P ≠ NP alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.
why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.

progress.text: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.

definitions: DistNP consists of pairs (L,D) with L in NP and D_n a polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from D_n have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.

importance.reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.
